metaData.originalTitle: Skill 文档也能训练？SkillOpt：把 Agent 的经验写进一份可优化说明书
metaData.title: Can Skill Documents Be Trained? SkillOpt: Turning Agent Experience into an Optimizable Manual
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: This article interprets Microsoft's paper SkillOpt, which proposes treating an Agent's Skill documents as trainable external states, enabling automated iterative optimization through mechanisms like rollout, reflection, bounded edits, and validation gates.
metaData.summary: This article provides a detailed interpretation of Microsoft's paper SkillOpt, which introduces a method for optimizing an Agent's Skill documents (i.e., prompts, manuals, or workflow specifications) as trainable external states. The article points out that traditional Skill documents are either written manually or generated by LLMs in a single pass, lacking a feedback loop. SkillOpt, in contrast, mimics the deep learning training paradigm by treating Skill documents as parameters and iteratively optimizing them in text space through mechanisms such as rollout (executing tasks), reflection (analyzing trajectories), bounded edits (constrained modifications), validation gates (verification), and rejected-edit buffers (negative feedback). Experimental results show that SkillOpt achieves optimal or tied-optimal performance across all 52 evaluation items, with significant improvements over baselines without Skills on multiple benchmarks, especially on tool-based tasks like Spreadsheet. The article also analyzes ablation study results for core components of SkillOpt (such as learning rate, rejected buffer, and slow update) and provides simplified recommendations for real-world implementation.

mainPoints.point: SkillOpt treats an Agent's Skill documents as trainable external states rather than static prompts.
mainPoints.explanation: The paper proposes that Skill documents should be repeatedly trained, validated, and iterated upon based on task feedback, much like model weights, to continuously improve the stability of Agent execution.

mainPoints.point: SkillOpt mimics the deep learning training paradigm, implementing a complete optimization pipeline in text space.
mainPoints.explanation: By leveraging mechanisms such as rollout (forward propagation), reflection (backward propagation), bounded edits (gradient updates), validation gates (verification), and rejected-edit buffers (negative feedback), a closed-loop Skill optimizer is constructed.

mainPoints.point: Experimental results show that SkillOpt achieves significant performance gains on multiple benchmarks, especially on tool-based tasks.
mainPoints.explanation: Achieving optimal or tied-optimal performance across all 52 evaluation items, with improvements of over 50 percentage points on tasks like Spreadsheet, demonstrates the method's effectiveness in operational tasks.

mainPoints.point: The engineering constraints of SkillOpt (such as learning rate, rejected buffer, and slow updates) are key to its success.
mainPoints.explanation: Ablation studies reveal that removing these constraints leads to substantial performance drops, indicating that SkillOpt's success is not solely due to LLM reflection but relies on rigorous engineering design.

keyQuotes: SkillOpt treats Skill documents as trainable external states, building an optimizer in text space using rollout, reflection, bounded edits, validation gates, and rejected buffers.

The most interesting part of this paper is how it seriously mimics the deep learning training paradigm. It doesn't just use 'training' as a metaphor; it actually finds textual counterparts for every step.
SkillOpt's success doesn't come from 'making the LLM reflect more times'; what really matters are several highly engineering-oriented constraints.
We used to say 'write experience into documents.' SkillOpt takes it a step further: treat documents as trainable experience.
